questions.q: A museum plaque must state how many years passed between the start of Harsha's rule at Kannauj and his death, using only the two dates in the chapter (606 CE and 647). A volunteer suggests the figure for Xuanzang's stay in India instead. Which figure should go on the plaque?
questions.a: 41 years: 647 - 606 = 41. The 14 years is Xuanzang's stay (630 to 644), 17 is 647 - 630, and 64 is the length of Amoghavarsha I's reign, which is a different ruler.
o: 41 years
14 years
17 years
64 years

questions.q: Meera's project covers two periods, the Gupta era and Harsha's reign, and she wants one Chinese pilgrim's account for each. Which pairing matches the chapter?
questions.a: Faxian left a valuable account of the Gupta era in the 5th century, and Xuanzang, two centuries later, travelled between 630 and 644 in Harsha's time. The other pairings swap them or use one pilgrim for both periods.
o: Faxian for the Guptas, Xuanzang for Harsha
Xuanzang for the Guptas, Faxian for Harsha
Xuanzang for both periods, since he travelled widely
Faxian for both periods, since he left a valuable account

questions.q: Xuanzang's travels in India ended in 644 and Harsha died in 647, so Harsha died ___ years after the pilgrim's travels in India ended.

Tanvi's group has four items: a copper plate carrying Harsha's signature, a coin with a peacock on the back, Bana's Harshacharita and Xuanzang's travelogue. They want the best source for how Kannauj looked to a visitor from outside India. Which should they use?
questions.a: Xuanzang's travelogue, because he was a visitor from China who described Kannauj as a beautiful and prosperous city. The signature and the coin do not describe the city, and Bana was a poet of Harsha's own court, not an outside visitor.
o: Xuanzang's travelogue
The copper plate with his signature
The coin with a peacock on its back
Bana's Harshacharita, a court biography

questions.q: A news reader says, 'Harsha's army swept beyond the Narmada and conquered the Deccan.' Which correction fits what the chapter says?
questions.a: The chapter says Harsha tried to extend his empire southward beyond the Narmada but was held in check by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty. The Tungabhadra boundary belongs to the later Pallava-Chalukya contest, the Palas rose after 750, and the Rashtrakutas occupied Kannauj only briefly, after Harsha's time.
o: Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas checked his southward push
The Pallavas of Kanchi turned his army back at the Tungabhadra
The Palas of Bengal drove his army out of the Deccan
The Rashtrakutas took Kannauj from him before 647

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harshavardhana.
1. His rule at Kannauj began in 606 CE.
2. Xuanzang described him as a ruler who stayed away from wars and kept only a small army.
3. Inscriptions show him as a devotee of Shiva, while other sources show him deeply attached to Buddhism.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Xuanzang described a just and energetic ruler who maintained a vast army and was often engaged in military campaigns.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Xuanzang's travelogue is a major source of information for historians of Harsha's period.
Reason (R): Xuanzang took more than 600 Buddhist manuscripts back to China.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. A holds because he left a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. The 600 manuscripts are a separate fact about his purpose, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kadambari  2. Harshacharita  3. Prayaga assembly  4. Varman dynasty of Kamarupa
Column B: a. an ally of Harsha in present-day Assam  b. held every five years, where much wealth was given away  c. a biography of Harsha  d. a novel completed by the author's son
questions.a: Kadambari is the novel that Bana left unfinished (d); Harshacharita is the biography (c); the Prayaga assembly was every five years (b); the Varmans of Kamarupa were allies (a). The distractors swap the novel with the biography or the assembly with the alliance.

questions.q: (a) For how many years did Xuanzang's travels in India last, going by the years the chapter gives? (b) If his 600 manuscripts were carried by 20 horses, what was the average number of manuscripts per horse?
questions.a: (a) 644 - 630 = 14 years. (b) 600 / 20 = 30 manuscripts per horse on average (the book says 'more than 600', so a little more than 30).
s: Part (a): 14 years from 630 to 644
Part (b): 600 divided by 20 gives 30 per horse

questions.q: True or False: Harsha's three Sanskrit plays are only 'stories', so a historian can learn nothing about the society of his time from them. Give a reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says historians use such literature to extract details about culture and society, from systems of governance to social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: historians draw details of governance, social diversity, technologies, foods and clothing from stories

questions.q: A classmate argues, 'Harsha honoured a Buddhist pilgrim, so he must have been a Buddhist ruler.' (a) What do the inscriptions and the other sources say about Harsha's own belief? (b) Why does this make the classmate's inference weak?
questions.a: (a) Inscriptions depict him as a devotee of Shiva, while other sources say he was also deeply attached to Buddhism. (b) He showed respect for all schools of thought and belief, so honouring one Buddhist visitor does not fix his own faith.
s: Part (a): Shiva devotee in inscriptions, deep attachment to Buddhism in other sources
Part (b): respect for all schools of thought, so one honour proves nothing about his own faith

questions.q: The chapter asks you to imagine you are a poor farmer watching the assembly at Prayaga. (a) What would you see happening, and how often does it take place? (b) Name the three groups the wealth was offered to and say which group you would belong to.
questions.a: (a) After performing sacred rites, Harsha gave away much wealth; the assembly was held every five years. (b) The wealth was offered to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor; a poor farmer would belong to the poor.
s: Part (a): sacred rites then giving away wealth, every five years
Part (b): Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor, and places the farmer among the poor

questions.q: A student writes, 'Harsha ruled from Sthaneshvara because his dynasty came from there.' (a) Correct the sentence. (b) Give one thing Xuanzang said about Kannauj and one thing he said about Harsha.
questions.a: (a) Harsha ruled from Kannauj, on the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh; Sthaneshvara (Thanesar in Haryana) was only his dynasty's earlier capital. (b) Xuanzang called Kannauj beautiful and prosperous, and Harsha a just and energetic ruler with a vast army, often on campaign.
s: Part (a): Kannauj as the capital he ruled from, Sthaneshvara as the earlier capital
Part (b): one detail on Kannauj and one on Harsha, both from Xuanzang

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Harsha signed as maharajadhiraja, the great king of kings, so his empire must have covered the whole subcontinent.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. A title in a signature does not prove the extent of an empire. The chapter says that its precise extent is not known with certainty, that Pulakeshin II held Harsha in check beyond the Narmada, and that he achieved only mixed success in uniting northern India.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since a title does not prove how far the empire reached
Cites that the extent is not known with certainty or that Pulakeshin II stopped him at the Narmada
Cites mixed success or continuing conflicts with neighbours in the north

questions.q: The chapter says Harsha 'achieved only mixed success' in uniting northern India. Support this with one success and two limits.
questions.a: Success: he expanded his empire over large parts of northern and eastern India and allied with the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa. Limits: Pulakeshin II held him in check beyond the Narmada; conflicts with neighbouring kingdoms continued; the Tripartite Struggle began soon after his death in 647.
s: One valid success (expansion over north and east, or the Varman alliance)
First limit stated correctly
Second limit stated correctly and different from the first

questions.q: Write three clues for a quiz so that the answer is 'Xuanzang'. One clue must carry a number, and each clue must use a different fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct clues, e.g. a Chinese pilgrim; he travelled in India between 630 and 644; he carried more than 600 manuscripts on 20 horses; Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj in his honour.
s: Clue 1 is correct and from the chapter
Clue 2 is correct and carries a number
Clue 3 is correct, new, and the clues together point to him alone

questions.q: 'Xuanzang's travelogue is a major source of information for historians of this period.' Justify this statement using his purpose, his journey, what he took back and what he recorded.
questions.a: He was a Chinese pilgrim who came, like Faxian before him, to visit sacred Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers. He travelled in the subcontinent between 630 and 644 and took back more than 600 Sanskrit manuscripts on 20 horses to translate into Chinese. He kept a meticulous account of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion in the kingdoms he crossed, including a picture of Kannauj as prosperous and Harsha as just and energetic. An eyewitness record of this kind is therefore a major source.
s: States his purpose: Buddhist sites and Indian teachers
Gives the dates 630 to 644 of the journey
Mentions the 600 manuscripts taken to China
Lists what he recorded: politics, diplomacy, culture, religion
Uses one detail on Harsha or Kannauj to show the value of the account

questions.q: Compare the assembly at Kannauj with the assembly at Prayaga under Harsha, and analyse what the two together show about him.
questions.a: The Kannauj assembly was held in honour of Xuanzang and was attended by kings and leaders of many religious sects. The Prayaga assembly, at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, was held every five years; after sacred rites Harsha gave away much wealth to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor. Together they show a king who honoured a foreign scholar, welcomed many beliefs and shared his wealth widely.
s: Purpose and guests of the Kannauj assembly
Frequency and setting of the Prayaga assembly
Recipients at Prayaga
A difference or similarity drawn between the two
Analysis: respect for many beliefs and generosity

questions.q:
The history club of a Pune school drafts a poster. It reads: 'A Chinese traveller came to India in 630 and left in 644. He came to trade silk. Harsha held an assembly at Kannauj for him and gave away riches at Prayaga every year.' The teacher asks the club to check the poster against the chapter.
(a) Find the two statements on the poster that the chapter does not support, and correct them.
(b) A visitor stays exactly in India from 630 to 644, both years included. At most how many five-yearly Prayaga assemblies could fall in these years?
(c) Name the kind of source the traveller's own writing is, and two things it recorded.
(d) The club can print only one headline: 'A Chinese Eye on Harsha's Court' or 'The King Who Gave Away His Wealth'. Choose one and justify it with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) Not to trade silk, but to visit Buddhist sites and learn from Indian teachers; and the Prayaga assembly was every five years, not every year. (b) At most 3 (for example 630, 635, 640), since a fourth would need 645. (c) A travelogue; it recorded politics, diplomacy, culture and religion. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the first draws on the travelogue and Kannauj assembly, the second on the five-yearly giving to Buddhists, Brahmins and the poor.
s: Part (a): corrects the trade motive and the yearly Prayaga claim
Part (b): at most 3 assemblies, with the working
Part (c): travelogue, with two things it recorded
Part (d): picks a headline and backs it with chapter evidence

questions.q:
Aarav finds a description of a 7th-century romance in his school library. A prince from Ujjayini loves a celestial being; their story passes through several births, dreams and divine realms, and tales are nested inside tales, with glimpses of palace life along the way. The author died before finishing it and someone else completed it. The same author also wrote a life of the king whose court he graced.
(a) Name the romance and its author, and say who completed it.
(b) Name the author's other work and say whom it is about.
(c) How many years after Harsha's rule began at Kannauj did Xuanzang's travels in India begin? Use the dates in the chapter.
(d) For a project on life in Harsha's court, would you take the romance or Xuanzang's travelogue as your main source? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Kadambari by Banabhatta (Bana); his son completed it. (b) Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha. (c) 630 - 606 = 24 years. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the romance gives glimpses of courtly life from inside the court, while the travelogue is an eyewitness record of politics, diplomacy, culture and religion but by an outsider.
s: Part (a): Kadambari, Bana, completed by his son
Part (b): Harshacharita, a biography of Harsha
Part (c): 630 - 606 = 24 years
Part (d): chooses one source and weighs its strength against its limit

questions.q: In the 9th century a Kannauj trader says, 'The city has changed hands again, but this time it is settled: one of the three rival powers will hold it for good.' Which reading of the Tripartite Struggle fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the three powers repeatedly warred against each other with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor. The Rashtrakutas briefly occupied Kannauj and later destroyed it, so they did not give up, and the Pratiharas lost Kannauj a century after Bhoja.
o: Outcomes kept swinging; no power won for good
The Palas held Kannauj once they won the first war
The Rashtrakutas gave up the contest for the Ganga plain
The Pratiharas kept Kannauj until the 11th century

questions.q: Harsha died in 647 and the people of Bengal chose Gopala in 750 CE, so Gopala was chosen ___ years after Harsha's death.
A school play shows Gopala seizing the throne of Bengal by force in 750 CE. Which corrected line is supported by the chapter?
questions.a: According to an inscription, Bengal fell into disorder after Harsha's death and the people chose Gopala in 750 CE to restore stability. He was the first Pala king; Dharmapala was his successor, and Harsha had died in 647.
o: The people chose him after a period of disorder
Dharmapala crowned him at Vikramashila after a war
He beat the Rashtrakutas in battle and took Bengal
Harsha appointed him governor of Bengal before 647

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'The Pala Empire was rich only because of its farms.' Which fact from the chapter points to another source of its wealth?
questions.a: The chapter says the Pala Empire flourished thanks to internal trade and brisk maritime trade through its east coast seaports, with pathways to Southeast Asia. The Kaveri delta belongs to the Cholas, the Kanchipuram trade to the Pallavas, and land grants are a general feature of the period, not a Pala source of wealth.
o: Maritime trade from its east coast seaports
Cash crops grown in the fertile Kaveri delta
Silk, spices and ivory traded through Kanchipuram
Land grants that created a new class of landholders

questions.q: Ishan's notes say, 'Dharmapala founded Nalanda, Vikramashila and Somapura.' What should his teacher correct?
questions.a: The chapter says Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, while the Palas, just like Harsha, continued to patronise Nalanda, which already existed. So Nalanda is the item to correct.
o: Nalanda: Palas only continued to patronise it
Somapura: it was really founded by Harsha at Kannauj
Vikramashila: it was actually a Chalukya foundation
Nothing needs correcting: Dharmapala founded all three

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Palas and the Tripartite Struggle.
1. The Palas won the Tripartite Struggle decisively and held Kannauj for ever.
2. Dharmapala was a great patron of Mahayana Buddhism.
3. The Pala Empire prospered through internal trade and through maritime trade from its east coast seaports.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the struggle was long and indecisive, with fluctuating outcomes and no lasting victor.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Several successors of Dharmapala patronised Buddhist institutions and yet were said to be devotees of Shiva.
Reason (R): In ancient India, except perhaps for monks and nuns, people could feel at ease with various belief systems and practise different modes of worship at the same time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. Because belief systems were fluid, a ruler could support Buddhist monasteries while worshipping Shiva.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Gopala  2. Dharmapala  3. Vikramashila  4. Bakhtiyar Khilji
Column B: a. plundered Vikramashila in the 12th century  b. chosen in 750 CE to restore stability in Bengal  c. a university with six colleges and scholar gatekeepers  d. expanded the Pala Empire and founded major monasteries
questions.a: Gopala was chosen in 750 CE (b); Dharmapala expanded the empire and founded monasteries (d); Vikramashila had six colleges with gatekeepers (c); Bakhtiyar Khilji plundered it (a). The distractors swap the two Pala kings or the university with its destroyer.

questions.q: Kavya's friend says, 'Three great powers would never fight for an ordinary town.' Using what the chapter tells us about Harsha's reign, give two reasons why Kannauj was worth fighting for.
questions.a: Harsha ruled from Kannauj from 606 CE, so it was the seat of a powerful king who hosted poets and scholars. Xuanzang described it as a beautiful and prosperous city, and Harsha held an assembly there attended by kings and leaders of many sects.
s: One reason: seat of Harsha's powerful kingdom or a city of scholars
Second reason: beautiful and prosperous city, or the great assembly held there

questions.q: True or False: Vikramashila admitted every applicant who reached its gates, since the Palas wanted learning to spread as widely as possible. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Admission was highly selective: each of the six colleges had a dvarapandita, a 'scholar gatekeeper', who tested students before allowing them entry.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: each college had a scholar gatekeeper who tested students before entry, so admission was highly selective

questions.q: (a) Who destroyed Vikramashila, according to the chapter, and in which century? (b) The university was founded in the late 8th century and was a great centre for more than four centuries. Show that its destruction in that century fits this.
questions.a: (a) Bakhtiyar Khilji plundered and destroyed it in the 12th century. (b) The late 8th century is about 780 to 800; adding more than 400 years gives about 1180 to 1200 or later, which lies in the 12th century.
s: Part (a): Bakhtiyar Khilji, 12th century
Part (b): late 8th century plus more than 400 years reaches the 12th century

questions.q: A student says, 'Monasteries like Vikramashila were only places of worship for monks.' Disagree using two facts about Vikramashila from the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says such large monasteries were in effect the universities of their time. Vikramashila had six colleges, lecture halls and a vast library, and nearly 3,000 scholars studied subjects such as grammar, logic and philosophy; it also attracted students from far away.
s: First fact: colleges, lecture halls or library showing a university
Second fact: subjects studied, number of scholars or students from afar

questions.q: True or False: Vikramashila's influence reached beyond India, because one of its famous teachers travelled to Tibet and translated Sanskrit works into Tibetan. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Vikramashila was especially known for its ties with Tibet; its teacher translated Sanskrit works into Tibetan and played a major role in shaping Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the teacher's translations into Tibetan shaped Tibetan Buddhism

questions.q: Meena says, 'The Pala kings patronised Buddhist institutions, but that does not mean every Pala king followed only Buddhism.' Is she right? Argue from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Dharmapala patronised Mahayana Buddhism and its monasteries, but the chapter notes that belief systems were fluid, that Harsha and the Guptas patronised several schools, and that several of Dharmapala's successors, while still patronising Buddhist institutions, were said to be devotees of Shiva.
s: Verdict: agrees, patronage did not mean following only Buddhism
Belief systems were fluid in ancient India
Successors patronised Buddhist institutions yet were Shiva devotees

questions.q: Explain three ways in which centres of learning such as Vikramashila served the Pala Empire and India's knowledge traditions.
questions.a: They drew numerous students, sometimes from far away and even from beyond India; they built links abroad, as with Tibet, whose Buddhism a Vikramashila teacher helped shape; and, with hundreds of such centres across India, they kept alive and enriched India's long-standing knowledge traditions, leaving a legacy of learning in eastern and northern India.
s: Attracted students from far away and beyond India
Links beyond India, such as the Tibetan connection
Kept alive and enriched India's knowledge traditions, a lasting legacy of learning

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Palas and the Rashtrakutas were already fighting each other for Kannauj in 640 CE.' Show with numbers and dates from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Pala dynasty began when Gopala was chosen in 750, which is 750 - 640 = 110 years after 640. Also Harsha was still ruling from Kannauj in 640 (he died in 647), and the Tripartite Struggle began only after his death, in the 8th and 9th centuries.
s: States that Harsha was alive in 640 and died in 647, and the struggle came after
Calculates 750 - 640 = 110 years before the first Pala king
Concludes that the Palas could not have fought for Kannauj in 640

questions.q: Compare the three parties of the Tripartite Struggle and analyse why the struggle for Kannauj ended without a lasting victor.
questions.a: The Palas came from the east, the Gurjara-Pratiharas from the west and the Rashtrakutas from the Deccan. After Harsha died in 647 Kannauj became the centre of a long struggle among them in the 8th and 9th centuries. The three powers repeatedly warred against each other with fluctuating outcomes. The rival states had comparable military strength, so none could keep Kannauj for long against the other two; there was no lasting victor and the struggle was indecisive.
s: Names the three powers
Gives their directions or regions
Gives the period and the prize, Kannauj
Describes the repeated wars with fluctuating results
Analysis: the rivals had comparable military strength, so no lasting victor

questions.q: 'The Pala Empire left a lasting legacy of strong governance and learning.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: Dharmapala expanded the empire and patronised Mahayana Buddhism by founding Vikramashila and Somapura and continuing to support Nalanda. These monasteries were the universities of the time and drew students from far, even from beyond India. Vikramashila had six colleges and a vast library, tested its applicants and had ties with Tibet. The empire also prospered through internal trade and east coast seaports. Even after its decline, it left a legacy of governance and learning in parts of eastern and northern India.
s: Dharmapala's expansion and patronage
Monasteries named: Vikramashila, Somapura, Nalanda
Students from far away and beyond India
Trade and economic strength behind it
Concludes with the legacy after decline

questions.q:
For a role-play on Vikramashila, a Patna school sets up one gate for each college of the university. Forty-eight Class 7 students act as applicants and are shared equally among the gates; a separate student stands at each gate as the gatekeeper. The teacher wants the numbers to match the chapter.
(a) Name the official the gatekeeper students are acting, and say what he did.
(b) According to the chapter, how many colleges did the university have, and so how many applicants stand at each gate?
(c) The chapter gives a figure for the scholars of the whole university. Using it, find the average number of scholars per college.
(d) The principal says a hard gate test will keep the numbers small, while an easy entry will let in students from far away who cannot take a long test. Which should the school's role-play follow? Decide, using what the chapter says about admission and about who came to study.
questions.a: (a) A dvarapandita, the scholar gatekeeper of a college, who tested students before allowing them in. (b) Six colleges, so 48 / 6 = 8 applicants at each gate (the gatekeepers are extra students). (c) Nearly 3,000 scholars / 6 = about 500 scholars per college. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: a hard test matches the highly selective admission of the real university; easy entry matches the way it attracted numerous students from far away, even beyond India.
s: Part (a): dvarapandita who tested students at the gate
Part (b): six colleges, so 48 divided by 6 gives 8
Part (c): nearly 3,000 scholars divided by 6 gives about 500
Part (d): decision justified with selective admission or students coming from afar

questions.q:
A Kolkata museum prepares a wall panel that begins: 'In 750 CE, after a period of confusion in the region, a leader was picked by the people to bring calm. The ruler who came after him won lands across the east and north, built two new centres of learning and went on helping an older one. Boats leaving the eastern coast kept the treasury full.' The museum can afford only one extra display.
(a) Name the first king and the dynasty he began, and name his successor.
(b) Name the two monasteries the successor founded.
(c) How did the ports on the east coast help the kingdom?
(d) The choice is between a model of a monastery gate scene and a case of goods that sailed to Southeast Asia. Which display better explains why the kingdom lasted for long? Decide, and justify with one fact from the chapter, noting one fact that supports the other display.
questions.a: (a) Gopala, who founded the Pala dynasty; his successor was Dharmapala. (b) Vikramashila (in Bihar) and Somapura (in Bangladesh). (c) They carried brisk maritime trade, giving pathways to Southeast Asia and adding to the empire's wealth. (d) Either display is acceptable if reasoned: the monastery scene rests on the monasteries as universities drawing students from far; the trade case rests on internal and maritime trade that enriched the empire. A fact from the other side must be noted.
s: Part (a): Gopala, Pala dynasty, successor Dharmapala
Part (b): Vikramashila and Somapura
Part (c): maritime trade with Southeast Asia from the east coast
Part (d): display chosen, justified, and a fact from the other side noted

questions.q: Rahul's notes say the Gurjara-Pratiharas first ruled from Ujjayini and later from Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal). His teacher asks him to fix the order using the chapter. What is the right order?
questions.a: The chapter says the early capital was Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal in western Rajasthan) and that it seems to have shifted later to Ujjayini. Manyakheta was a Rashtrakuta capital, and Kannauj was the prize of the struggle, not their first capital.
o: Bhillamala first, then apparently Ujjayini
Ujjayini first, then Bhillamala (Bhinmal)
Kannauj first, then Bhillamala (Bhinmal)
Bhillamala first, then Manyakheta (Malkheda)

questions.q: A quiz asks, 'Who built the empire stretching from Punjab and Kathiawar in the west to Kannauj in the east?' A student answers 'Nagabhata I, the founder of the dynasty.' What is the right correction?
questions.a: Nagabhata I founded the dynasty in the mid-8th century, but it was the celebrated 9th-century ruler Bhoja who built the empire reaching from Punjab and Kathiawar to Kannauj. Dantidurga and Krishna I were Rashtrakutas.
o: It was Bhoja, in the 9th century, not the founder
It was Dantidurga, who overthrew the Chalukyas
It was Krishna I, who had the Ellora temple carved
Nothing to correct; the founder also built the empire

questions.q: Bhoja's empire belongs to the 9th century. The chapter says Kannauj was destroyed by Rashtrakuta rulers a century later, so this happened in the ___ century.
questions.a: 10th

questions.q: Pooja notices 'Nrupatunga Road' in central Bengaluru and asks whom it commemorates. Going by the chapter, which ruler should the guide name?
questions.a: The chapter says Nrupatunga Road is named after Amoghavarsha I, who took the title 'Nripatunga' ('peak of kings') and whose reign lasted 64 years. Krishna I, Dantidurga and Bhoja are other rulers from the same section.
o: Amoghavarsha I, who reigned 64 years
Krishna I, who had the Ellora temple carved
Dantidurga, the first independent ruler
Bhoja, also known as Mihira

questions.q: A coin collector in Jaipur shows a silver coin about 2 cm across, with Varaha, the boar avatar of Vishnu, on it. The guide says the best-known king of this dynasty even took the name Adi Varaha. Which dynasty issued such coins?
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, whose celebrated king Bhoja was a devotee of Vishnu and was also called Adi Varaha. The Palas, Rashtrakutas and Chalukyas are not linked with this coin in the chapter.
o: The Gurjara-Pratiharas
The Rashtrakutas
The Palas
The Chalukyas of Badami

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Bhoja built an empire stretching from Punjab and Kathiawar in the west to Kannauj in the east.
2. The Gurjara-Pratihara empire was finally eliminated by the Rashtrakutas.

questions.a: Only 1 is correct. The Gurjara-Pratiharas were finally eliminated by the Ghaznavids in the early 11th century, although a Rashtrakuta attack destroyed Kannauj. Amoghavarsha I also patronised Hindu temples.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Kailashanatha temple at Ellora is described as a gigantic sculpture and not as a construction.
Reason (R): It is the largest rock-cut temple in India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but being the largest does not explain why it is called a sculpture. The explanation is that it was carved out of a hillside.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each ruler in Column A with his description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Nagabhata I  2. Bhoja  3. Dantidurga  4. Krishna I
Column B: a. first independent Rashtrakuta ruler, who overthrew the Chalukyas  b. founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty  c. had the Kailashanatha temple carved at Ellora  d. a devotee of Vishnu whose empire reached from Punjab to Kannauj
questions.a: Nagabhata I founded the Gurjara-Pratiharas (b), Bhoja built their great empire (d), Dantidurga was the first independent Rashtrakuta (a) and Krishna I got the Ellora temple made (c). Distractors swap founders with the great kings of the same dynasty.

questions.q: True or False: The Rashtrakutas supported only Jain scholars, because Amoghavarsha I is sometimes called a 'Jain king'. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Rashtrakutas equally patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools of thought, and Amoghavarsha I, though strongly drawn to Jainism, also patronised Hindu temples.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: equal patronage of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools; Amoghavarsha I also patronised Hindu temples

questions.q: (a) What title did Amoghavarsha I take, and what does it mean? (b) The chapter says he ensured peace and prosperity despite frequent wars, and also a third quality because of the length of his reign. Name the quality and the length.
questions.a: (a) 'Nripatunga', meaning 'peak of kings'. (b) Stability, since his reign lasted 64 years.
s: Part (a): Nripatunga, peak of kings
Part (b): stability, with a reign of 64 years

questions.q: Show how the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas each came into the story of Kannauj, one point for each dynasty.
questions.a: Under Bhoja the Gurjara-Pratihara empire stretched to Kannauj and controlled most of north India. Rashtrakuta rulers campaigned successfully in north India and briefly occupied Kannauj; later they destroyed it.
s: Pratihara link: Bhoja's empire reached Kannauj
Rashtrakuta link: briefly occupied (and later destroyed) Kannauj

questions.q: (a) A 10th-century Arab historian praised a Rashtrakuta ruler, saying Islam was honoured in his kingdom and mosques were always full. What does the remark tell us about the Rashtrakutas? (b) Why should a historian not build the dynasty's whole religious policy on this one remark?
questions.a: (a) It suggests the Rashtrakutas respected and protected Muslims, in line with their patronage of many faiths. (b) It is a single outsider's account; it should be checked against other evidence, such as their equal patronage of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools.
s: Part (a): the ruler respected and protected Muslims in his kingdom
Part (b): one outside remark needs other evidence before it describes a whole policy

questions.q: A teacher at Malkheda in Karnataka says the town was once the capital of a dynasty that dominated for nearly two centuries. (a) Name the dynasty and the old name of the town. (b) Which dynasty did it replace in the Deccan, and who began the replacement?
questions.a: (a) The Rashtrakutas; the town was Manyakheta. (b) It replaced the Chalukyas, when Dantidurga overthrew them in the mid-8th century.
s: Part (a): Rashtrakutas and Manyakheta
Part (b): replaced the Chalukyas, begun by Dantidurga

questions.q: Dev says, 'A dynasty that fought many wars could still find the time and money to create great works.' Is he right? Test this claim using the Rashtrakutas.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter warns us not to imagine such kings as constantly at war: the Rashtrakutas campaigned in north India and Amoghavarsha I fought frequent wars, yet Krishna I got the Kailashanatha temple, the largest rock-cut temple in India, carved at Ellora, and Amoghavarsha I ensured peace and prosperity for 64 years and was a poet in Sanskrit and Kannada.
s: Verdict: agrees, wars did not stop great works
Evidence of wars or campaigns in the north
Evidence of building or culture: Kailashanatha temple, or peace and poetry under Amoghavarsha I

questions.q: A student draws a graph of Gurjara-Pratihara power: rising in the mid-8th century, high in the 9th, falling sharply a century later and ending in the early 11th. Justify each turn of the graph with one fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Rise: Nagabhata I founded the dynasty in the mid-8th century. High point: in the 9th century Bhoja built an empire from Punjab and Kathiawar to Kannauj, controlling most of north India. Fall: a century later Rashtrakuta rulers destroyed Kannauj, which hastened the empire's disintegration; the Ghaznavids finally eliminated it in the early 11th century.
s: Rise: founded by Nagabhata I in the mid-8th century
High point: Bhoja's empire in the 9th century
Fall: Kannauj destroyed by the Rashtrakutas, then final elimination by the Ghaznavids

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'Bhoja'. Write three clues, each using a different fact from the chapter, so that the third clue alone rules out Nagabhata I.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct clues, e.g. a devotee of Vishnu; also known as Mihira and Adi Varaha; his empire stretched from Punjab and Kathiawar to Kannauj in the 9th century. The third clue must be one that only fits Bhoja, such as the 9th-century empire reaching Kannauj.
s: Clue 1 is correct and from the chapter
Clue 2 is correct and a different fact
Clue 3 is correct, new, and fits Bhoja but not Nagabhata I

questions.q: Compare the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas under these heads: origin and founder, capital, greatest period, and patronage. Then say which of the two the chapter shows leaving more lasting monuments.
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were founded by Nagabhata I in the mid-8th century, probably from the Gurjara region of western India, with capitals first at Bhillamala and later Ujjayini; under Bhoja they held most of north India. The Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga, who overthrew the Chalukyas, with their capital at Manyakheta in Karnataka, and were dominant for nearly two centuries; they patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools and Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada. The chapter shows the Rashtrakutas leaving the more lasting monument, the Kailashanatha temple at Ellora.
s: Origin and founders of both dynasties
Capitals of both
Greatest period or extent of each
Patronage by the Rashtrakutas (and the Pratihara devotion to Vishnu)
Conclusion naming the Ellora temple as the lasting monument

questions.q: 'Amoghavarsha I was a ruler of peace and culture even though he fought frequent wars.' Justify this statement from the chapter.
questions.a: He fought frequent wars with neighbouring kingdoms, including the dynasties surveyed earlier, yet managed to ensure peace, prosperity and stability within his empire. His reign lasted 64 years. He took the title Nripatunga, 'peak of kings'. He was drawn to Jainism, which is why he is sometimes called a 'Jain king', but he also patronised Hindu temples. He was a fine poet who composed in Sanskrit and Kannada, and a road in Bengaluru is still named after him.
s: Acknowledges the frequent wars
Peace and prosperity for 64 years
Religious patronage: Jainism and Hindu temples
Poet in Sanskrit and Kannada
Lasting memory such as the title or Nrupatunga Road

questions.q:
A Class 7 group visits Ellora in Maharashtra to see a famous temple. The guide says: 'This temple was made for a king of the dynasty that overthrew the Chalukyas in the Deccan.' Later the group's teacher adds that the same dynasty fought many wars and campaigned as far as the north.
(a) Name the temple and the king who got it made.
(b) Name the three traditions and the three languages the dynasty supported.
(c) The chapter's caption calls the temple 'not a construction but a gigantic sculpture' carved out of a hillside. What does this suggest about the wealth and skill the dynasty could command, despite its wars?
(d) A minister argues that the money should have gone to the army instead. Give one point for the minister and one for the king, and say which is stronger.
questions.a: (a) The Kailashanatha temple, got made by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. (b) Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions; Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada. (c) Carving a whole temple out of a hillside as one sculpture needed great resources, labour and skill, so the dynasty could spare both despite its wars; the chapter says such kings found time and resources to create wonders. (d) Minister: the dynasty fought many wars and was dominant for nearly two centuries because of its army; king: the dynasty was not constantly at war and its wonders are what we remember. Either verdict is acceptable if reasoned.
s: Part (a): Kailashanatha temple and Krishna I
Part (b): three traditions and three languages
Part (c): carving a hillside into a temple shows great resources and skill
Part (d): one point each side and a reasoned verdict

questions.q:
A heritage walk in Kannauj has a board that reads: 'In the 9th century a king devoted to Vishnu, also called Mihira and Adi Varaha, made this city the eastern end of an empire that ran from Punjab and Kathiawar. A century later southern rulers destroyed the city, and early in the 11th century an invader finished off his dynasty.'
(a) Name the king and his dynasty.
(b) Which dynasty destroyed Kannauj, and who finally eliminated the empire?
(c) Counting from the century of the king's empire to the century of final elimination, how many centuries passed?
(d) The guide must pick one cause to stress: the destruction of Kannauj by the southern rulers or the final blow by the invader. Decide, using the chapter's wording.
questions.a: (a) Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. (b) The Rashtrakutas destroyed Kannauj; the Ghaznavids finally eliminated the empire. (c) 11 - 9 = 2 centuries. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the destruction of Kannauj 'hastened the disintegration' of the empire, so it started the decline, while the Ghaznavids 'finally eliminated' it, so they ended it.
s: Part (a): Bhoja and the Gurjara-Pratiharas
Part (b): Rashtrakutas destroyed Kannauj; Ghaznavids finally eliminated the empire
Part (c): 11 - 9 = 2 centuries
Part (d): picks a cause and justifies it with the chapter's wording

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kalhana  2. Abhinavagupta  3. Lalitaditya Muktapida  4. Didda
Column B: a. a Karkota ruler seen as firm  b. a Kashmir Shaivism scholar who wrote on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics  c. a late 10th-century queen who removed rivals, even her grandsons  d. the Kashmiri poet who composed the Rajatarangini in the 12th century
questions.a: Kalhana composed the Rajatarangini (d); Abhinavagupta was the Kashmir Shaivism scholar (b); Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty is seen as a firm ruler (a); Didda was the late 10th-century queen (c). The distractors swap the poet with the scholar or the king with the queen.

questions.q: Sara is writing a note on Queen Didda for a class display. The chapter attributes the account of how she held power to Kalhana. Which wording is the most careful?
questions.a: The chapter says that, according to Kalhana, Didda consolidated power through alliances and by ruthlessly eliminating rivals, including her own grandsons, so the careful note names its source. It does not say every source agrees, she built temples as well as removing rivals, and she lived in the late 10th century, not the 12th.
o: According to Kalhana, she removed rivals, even grandsons
As every source agrees, she removed rivals, even grandsons
She never harmed rivals, as she built many temples
She removed rivals in the 12th century, as Kalhana wrote

questions.q: Queen Didda consolidated her power in the late 10th century and Kalhana composed the Rajatarangini in the 12th, so the poem was written about ___ centuries after her time.
Imran's teacher says a historian should be 'like a judge', as Kalhana wished. Which action best follows that ideal?
questions.a: Kalhana said a poet is worthy of praise only if his words, like a judge's, remain free from love or hatred in relating the facts of the past. The other actions favour the king, hide facts or ignore the earlier works and writings Kalhana also consulted.
o: Record deeds without love or hatred
Praise the ruling king so that he stays pleased
Leave out events that shame a famous dynasty
Use only the rulers' own inscriptions as proof

questions.q: Pooja reads Kalhana's lines: 'Those who are intent on harassing their subjects perish with their families; fortune waits on the descendants of those who reinstate order where there is chaos.' What does this show about his purpose?
questions.a: He wanted to draw moral lessons from history by highlighting the rulers' ethical values. The chapter does not describe him as a recorder of battle dates, a praiser of artisans or a teacher of advaita; that is Shankaracharya's teaching.
o: To draw moral lessons from the rulers' conduct
To praise the artists and artisans of Kashmir
To record the dates of each battle fought
To explain the teaching that the world is maya

questions.q: A librarian finds three manuscripts by a Kashmiri scholar on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics. Under which school of thought should she shelve them, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says Kashmir Shaivism produced great scholars such as Abhinavagupta, whose works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics had a vast influence across India. Advaita vedanta is Shankaracharya's school, and the Buddhist schools are different traditions.
o: Kashmir Shaivism
Advaita vedanta
Mahayana Buddhism
Vajrayana Buddhism

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Kalhana says he examined eleven earlier works and consulted inscriptions before writing.
2. Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty is seen as a firm ruler.
3. Shankaracharya established all four of his mathas in the Kashmir valley near Srinagar.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: his four mathas stood at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri, in four different corners of India.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Kalhana tried to make his account of Kashmir's kings reliable by checking earlier works and inscriptions.
Reason (R): Kalhana held that a writer of history should be moved by love or hatred for the persons of the past.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: he examined eleven earlier works and consulted inscriptions and other writings to overcome errors. R is false: he said a worthy writer's words, like a judge's, must remain free from love or hatred.

questions.q: True or False: Because the chapter says Shankaracharya visited the hill overlooking Srinagar, he set up one of his four mathas there. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says only that, according to tradition, he visited the hill; his four mathas were at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the visit is a tradition, and the four mathas stood at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri

questions.q: (a) Name two of the four places where Shankaracharya established mathas. (b) The chapter asks why he chose four different corners of India rather than central places. Give one reasoned answer and say whether the chapter itself supplies one.
questions.a: (a) Any two of Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri. (b) The chapter only poses the question and gives no answer, so any reasoned answer is accepted, e.g. mathas at four corners could carry his teaching to every region.
s: Part (a): two correct places among Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri
Part (b): a reasoned answer, noting that the chapter poses but does not answer the question

questions.q: Differentiate Shankaracharya's school from Kashmir Shaivism by saying what each is known for in the chapter.
questions.a: Shankaracharya taught advaita vedanta: brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness and the world we perceive is maya, an illusion. Kashmir Shaivism produced scholars such as Abhinavagupta, whose works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics were widely influential.
s: Shankaracharya: brahman as ultimate reality and the perceived world as maya
Kashmir Shaivism: scholars such as Abhinavagupta and their works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics

questions.q: A monk from Tibet in this period wants to study Buddhist manuscripts and also have a copy of a text painted by a skilled artist. (a) To which region of India would the chapter send him for the manuscripts, and why was it a good choice? (b) Why could he expect to find a manuscript painter there?
questions.a: (a) Kashmir, which was a crucial bridge for Buddhist scholarship: scholars, monks and texts travelled between Kashmir, other parts of northern India, Tibet and Central Asia. (b) Kashmir's artisans, sculptors and manuscript painters were in demand across north India and beyond.
s: Part (a): Kashmir, a bridge for Buddhist scholarship linking Tibet and Central Asia
Part (b): manuscript painters and artisans of Kashmir were in demand

questions.q: Compare Lalitaditya Muktapida and Queen Didda as the Rajatarangini presents them, one point each.
questions.a: Lalitaditya of the Karkota dynasty is seen as a firm ruler. After him Kashmir saw conflicts, and in the late 10th century Didda consolidated power through alliances and by ruthlessly eliminating rivals, including her own grandsons, while also founding towns and building and restoring temples.
s: Lalitaditya: a firm ruler of the Karkota dynasty
Didda: alliances and ruthless elimination of rivals, with towns and temples

questions.q: Zoya says, 'Kashmir lay behind high mountains, so it had little part in the culture of the rest of India.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that despite its mountainous geography Kashmir remained well connected to developments elsewhere. It was a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy and arts, and Abhinavagupta's works influenced all of India. It was also a bridge for Buddhist scholarship and its artisans were in demand across north India.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since Kashmir stayed connected despite the mountains
Learning, philosophy and Abhinavagupta's wide influence
Buddhist bridge or artisans in demand beyond Kashmir

questions.q: Rina says, 'Queen Didda was a ruthless schemer and nothing more.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. According to Kalhana she did consolidate power by ruthlessly eliminating rivals, including her own grandsons. But 'nothing more' is wrong: she also made strategic alliances, founded a few towns, built several temples and restored many more.
s: Verdict: partly right
The part that holds: ruthless elimination of rivals, as Kalhana tells it
The part that fails: alliances, towns founded and temples built or restored

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because he wanted to draw moral lessons from the ethical values of rulers.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and give two examples from the chapter that show this purpose at work.
questions.a: Question: Why did Kalhana describe rulers' conduct in the Rajatarangini? Examples: his lines that those who harass their subjects perish with their families while fortune waits on those who reinstate order; his account of Queen Didda's ruthless elimination of rivals.
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First example from the chapter
Second, different example

questions.q: 'Kalhana's method was careful, but his aim was more than recording facts.' Justify this statement, using his sources, his stated ideals and his purpose.
questions.a: Kalhana, a Kashmiri scholar-poet, wrote the Rajatarangini in Sanskrit in the 12th century. He examined eleven earlier works and consulted inscriptions about temple consecrations, royal grants and praise records, which shows care in checking sources. He said that a worthy writer must be free from love or hatred like a judge. Yet his purpose went beyond records: he highlighted the rulers' ethical values to draw moral lessons, as in his lines that those who harass their subjects perish with their families.
s: Who he was, what he wrote, and when
Eleven earlier works examined
Inscriptions and written works consulted
The ideal of being free from love or hatred
Moral purpose with a quoted example

questions.q: 'Despite its mountains, Kashmir was part of the cultural life of the whole subcontinent.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: The chapter says Kashmir remained well connected to political and cultural developments elsewhere. It was a major centre of Sanskrit learning, philosophy and the arts. The school of Kashmir Shaivism produced scholars like Abhinavagupta, whose works on philosophy, poetry, arts and aesthetics had a vast influence across India. It was a crucial bridge for Buddhist scholarship as scholars, monks and texts travelled between Kashmir, other parts of northern India, Tibet and Central Asia. Its artisans, sculptors and manuscript painters were in demand across north India and beyond.
s: Stays connected despite mountains
Sanskrit learning and philosophy
Abhinavagupta and Kashmir Shaivism with wide influence
Bridge for Buddhist scholarship to Tibet and Central Asia
Artisans, sculptors and painters in demand beyond Kashmir

questions.q:
A Class 7 history club reads a line by a 12th-century Kashmiri scholar: 'I went through eleven earlier works, and by studying inscriptions and other writings I got past many difficulties caused by mistakes.' Ananya says his method makes his book reliable. Rohit says his praise and blame of kings makes it biased.
(a) Name the scholar and the book.
(b) Name two kinds of inscriptions he consulted, according to the chapter.
(c) Give one way in which his method resembles the way history is checked today (any reasonable comparison is accepted).
(d) For a school project on Kashmir's rulers, would you rely on his book? Decide and justify, using both Ananya's and Rohit's points.
questions.a: (a) Kalhana and the Rajatarangini. (b) Any two of inscriptions relating to temple consecrations, royal grants and laudatory records. (c) Any reasonable comparison, e.g. he cross-checked many earlier works and inscriptions, as historians compare sources today. (d) A reasoned judgement such as: rely on it, but cross-check, since the method is careful but he also meant to draw moral lessons from rulers' conduct.
s: Part (a): Kalhana, Rajatarangini
Part (b): two kinds of inscriptions
Part (c): cross-checking many sources
Part (d): decision using both students' points

questions.q:
A guide on the hill above Srinagar (also called Takht-i-Sulaiman, once Gopadri) tells visitors: 'The great 8th-century teacher of advaita vedanta stood right here, and his four monasteries all stand in this valley.' A stone temple at the top is known by two names. The local council can add only one new board: one on the four monasteries, or one on the scholars of Kashmir Shaivism.
(a) Name the teacher and say what he taught about brahman and about the world.
(b) Correct the guide's statement about his four monasteries.
(c) The chapter says he visited the hill 'according to tradition'. What does this wording ask of the guide?
(d) Decide which board the council should add for visitors to Kashmir, and justify your choice with chapter evidence for one board and one point in favour of the other.
questions.a: (a) Adi Shankaracharya; brahman is the ultimate reality or pure consciousness, and the world as we perceive it is maya, an illusion. (b) His four mathas stood at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri, not in the valley. (c) To say that the visit is a tradition and not a proven fact. (d) Either board is acceptable if reasoned: the matha board shows his reach across four corners of India; the Kashmir Shaivism board shows Kashmir's own scholars such as Abhinavagupta, whose works influenced all India.
s: Part (a): Shankaracharya; brahman as ultimate reality; the world as maya
Part (b): mathas at Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka and Sringeri, not in the valley
Part (c): the visit is a tradition, so the guide should speak with that caution
Part (d): chooses a board, justifies it, and notes a point for the other

questions.q: A student says, 'After Narasimhavarman I captured Badami, he kept it and made it part of the Pallava kingdom for good.' Which statement from the chapter corrects him?
questions.a: The chapter says Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakeshin II and went on to capture Badami, but then retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra River as an unwritten boundary between the two powers. It does not say he was driven out, and the Rashtrakutas replaced the Chalukyas only by the mid-8th century.
o: He retreated behind the Tungabhadra boundary
Pulakeshin II drove him out within a single year
The Rashtrakutas drove him out soon afterwards
He stayed on and made Badami a second capital

questions.q: The Chalukya dynasty was founded in the mid-6th century and the Rashtrakutas had replaced it in the Deccan by the mid-8th century, so the Chalukyas of Badami lasted about ___ years.

Neha's school trip has two stops. Stop one is the later capital of the Chalukyas, famous for its complex of Hindu and Jain cave temples. Stop two is their earlier capital, with over a hundred temples and a hill temple carrying a long inscription. Which pair of present-day places is right?
questions.a: Vatapi, present-day Badami, was the capital famous for its cave temples, and the earlier capital Aryapura is present-day Aihole with over a hundred temples and the Meguti temple inscription. Basavakalyan (Kalyani) and Vengi belong to the later Western and Eastern branches.
o: Badami, then Aihole
Aihole, then Badami
Basavakalyan, then Vengi
Basavakalyan, then Aihole

questions.a: The chapter says the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, as some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions. It does not say it is unreadable, late or hostile.
o: Parts of it are contradicted by other inscriptions
It was written centuries later by a foreign pilgrim
It is in a script nobody can read today
It praises Harsha and finds fault with Pulakeshin II

questions.q: Archaeologists digging at Mamallapuram find old Chinese, Persian and Roman coins. What does the chapter let us conclude?
questions.a: Mamallapuram was a Pallava seaport in trade with distant lands. The coins do not show conquest, nor that the Pallavas minted foreign money, nor that a visitor left them.
o: It was a seaport trading with distant lands
The Pallavas conquered China, Persia and Rome
The Pallavas minted coins on foreign designs
Chalukya traders from Aihole had brought them home

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
2. Narasimhavarman I was also known as 'Mamalla', which means 'wrestler' or 'warrior'.

questions.a: All three are in the chapter, so none of the statements is false.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After capturing Badami, Narasimhavarman I made it a permanent part of the Pallava kingdom.
Reason (R): After capturing Badami he retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra River as an unwritten boundary between the two powers.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
