questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the right description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Ravikirti  2. Mamalla  3. Dandin  4. Vengi
Column B: a. court poet who praised Pulakeshin II at Aihole  b. title of Narasimhavarman I, meaning wrestler or warrior  c. poet of elaborate Sanskrit poetry hosted by the Pallavas  d. capital of the Eastern Chalukyas
questions.a: Ravikirti praised Pulakeshin II (a); Mamalla was Narasimhavarman I's name (b); Dandin was a Sanskrit poet at the Pallava court (c); Vengi was the Eastern Chalukya capital (d). The distractors swap the two poets, one from each dynasty.

questions.q: True or False: Pulakeshin II, who held Harsha in check beyond the Narmada, was himself later defeated, and the victors were the Pallavas of Kanchi. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Pulakeshin II eventually tasted defeat at the hands of the Pallavas; it was Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) who defeated him and went on to capture Badami.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Narasimhavarman I of the Pallavas defeated him and captured Badami

questions.q: (a) Name the languages whose literature the Pallavas promoted and those promoted under the Eastern Chalukyas. (b) How many of these four languages are regional languages rather than Sanskrit, and what does that suggest about literature in this period?
questions.a: (a) The Pallavas promoted Sanskrit and Tamil; the Eastern Chalukyas, Telugu and Kannada literature. (b) Three of the four (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada) are regional languages, which suggests that literature in regional languages flourished alongside Sanskrit.
s: Part (a): Sanskrit and Tamil for the Pallavas; Telugu and Kannada for the Eastern Chalukyas
Part (b): three of four are regional, so regional literature flourished alongside Sanskrit

questions.q: A guide at Mamallapuram says, 'This Shore Temple was built in the reign of Narasimhavarman I, who captured Badami.' (a) Correct the king, using what the chapter says about the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram. (b) What kinds of structures does the chapter say were carved at Mamallapuram?
questions.a: (a) The chapter says the Shore Temple was built during the reign of Narasimhavarman II of the Pallava dynasty, not Narasimhavarman I. (b) Elaborate rock-cut caves and monolithic temples, depicting deities or scenes from the Mahabharata.
s: Part (a): Narasimhavarman II, not Narasimhavarman I
Part (b): rock-cut caves and monolithic temples depicting deities or Mahabharata scenes

questions.q: Differentiate between the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Eastern Chalukyas.
questions.a: The Western Chalukyas were a revival of the dynasty in the west from the 10th century onward, with their capital at Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan in northern Karnataka). The Eastern Chalukyas were an eastern branch that became independent as the Badami empire declined, ruling from Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
s: Western Chalukyas: 10th century revival, capital Kalyani
Eastern Chalukyas: branch ruling from Vengi in Andhra Pradesh

questions.q: (a) What was the purpose of the naval expedition that Narasimhavarman I sent to Sri Lanka? (b) Give one other fact from the chapter that shows the Pallavas looked across the sea.
questions.a: (a) To help a Sinhalese prince recover his lost throne. (b) Any one: trade relations with Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia through seaports, especially Mamallapuram; ancient Chinese, Persian and Roman coins found there.
s: Part (a): helping a Sinhalese prince recover his lost throne
Part (b): sea trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, or the foreign coins at Mamallapuram

questions.q: Aarav says, 'Ravikirti's inscription praises Pulakeshin II too highly, so it is useless as evidence.' Is he completely right, partly right or wrong? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, since some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions, so it cannot be trusted blindly. But it is not useless: there is no doubt that in the early 7th century most of India was dominated by Harsha north of the Vindhyas and Pulakeshin II south of them, so some of its content can be accepted after cross-checking.
s: Verdict: partly right, since the inscription needs checking but is not useless
Poetical style and exaggerations contradicted by other inscriptions
Acknowledges that the two imperial powers claim is still accepted

questions.q: Using three facts from the chapter, show that Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram were centres of trade as well as of culture.
questions.a: Kanchipuram traded in spices, textiles including silk, ivory and other luxury goods. The Pallavas had trade relations with Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia through seaports, particularly Mamallapuram. Ancient Chinese, Persian and Roman coins were found there in excavations.
s: Goods traded at Kanchipuram
Trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia via seaports
Foreign coins found at Mamallapuram

questions.q: A student writes, 'By the mid-8th century the Pallavas had replaced the Chalukyas as rulers of the Deccan.' Show from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says that by the mid-8th century it was the Rashtrakutas who replaced the Chalukyas in the Deccan. The Pallavas, after capturing Badami, retreated to keep the Tungabhadra as a boundary, and they themselves were overthrown in the late 9th century by the Chola king Aditya I.
s: States that the Rashtrakutas replaced the Chalukyas
Notes that the Pallavas held Badami only briefly, since they retreated to the Tungabhadra boundary
Pallavas were themselves overthrown by Aditya I in the late 9th century

questions.q: Compare the Chalukyas and the Pallavas under these heads: founder or greatest king, capital, the clash between them, and patronage of religion and literature (for the Chalukyas' literature, use the Eastern Chalukyas).
questions.a: The Chalukyas were founded by Pulakeshin I in the mid-6th century and expanded under his grandson Pulakeshin II, with the capital first at Aryapura and later at Vatapi. The Pallavas, with their capital at Kanchi, peaked under Mahendravarman I and his son Narasimhavarman I. Pulakeshin II was defeated by the Pallavas and Narasimhavarman I captured Badami, though he retreated. Both patronised Hindu, Jain and other schools: the Pallavas promoted Sanskrit and Tamil literature and the Eastern Chalukyas Telugu and Kannada.
s: Founder or greatest king of each
Capitals of each
Their clash and its result
Religious patronage of each
Literary patronage of each

questions.q: 'A historian must read different sources together.' Justify this using the Meguti inscription at Aihole and Xuanzang's remarks on the Chalukya kingdom and on Kanchi.
questions.a: The inscription by Ravikirti praises Pulakeshin II in a highly poetical style and records his victories over Harsha and rival kings, but some facts it presents are contradicted by other inscriptions, so it is exaggerated. Xuanzang, an outsider, wrote that the king's beneficent actions are felt over a great distance and that his subjects obey him with perfect submission. At Kanchi he gave figures of 100 monasteries and 10,000 priests which are likely exaggerated, but also noted 80 Hindu temples, many Jains and the people's attachment to honesty and learning. Each source has strengths and flaws, so they must be read together.
s: The inscription and its exaggerations
Contradiction by other inscriptions
Xuanzang's remark on Pulakeshin II
Xuanzang's figures and remarks on Kanchi
Conclusion: sources have to be read together

questions.q:
A school heritage trail in Karnataka has three hours at Aihole. The trail leader has read that the site was once the earlier capital of a dynasty that later ruled from a place with famous cave temples, and that a long inscription stands on a hill temple there. The leader must plan the visit.
(a) Name the dynasty and give the old name of Aihole.
(b) Name the three traditions whose temples the chapter says stand at Aihole.
(c) At the Meguti temple the group will read a long inscription. Name its poet and the king it praises, and say why the guide warns that it must be cross-checked.
(d) With only three hours, should the group spend the longest time on the inscription or on walking through as many temples as possible? Decide, using what the chapter says each can teach.
questions.a: (a) The Chalukyas; Aryapura (later Ayyavole). (b) Hindu, Buddhist and Jain. (c) Ravikirti, the court poet, praising Pulakeshin II; the inscription is highly poetical and not free from exaggeration, and some of its facts are contradicted by other inscriptions. (d) Either choice is acceptable if reasoned: the inscription teaches about Pulakeshin II's victories, and how a historian tests a source; the temples show the Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions side by side at one site.
s: Part (a): Chalukyas and Aryapura
Part (b): Hindu, Buddhist and Jain temples
Part (c): Ravikirti, Pulakeshin II, and the exaggeration contradicted elsewhere
Part (d): decision tied to what the inscription or the temples teach

questions.q:
A Chinese pilgrim who visited the Pallava capital in the 7th century counted 100 Buddhist monasteries with 10,000 priests there, besides 80 Hindu temples and many Jains. A textbook adds that these figures are likely exaggerated. About the people he wrote that they are 'deeply attached to the principles of honesty and truth' and 'highly esteem learning'.
(a) Name the pilgrim and the present-day name of the capital.
(b) Name the two Pallava kings, father and son, under whom the dynasty reached its peak.
(c) Which parts of the pilgrim's account would you still accept even if the figures are exaggerated?
(d) A museum wants to use the account on a panel titled 'A City of Many Faiths'. Should it print the numbers? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Xuanzang; Kanchipuram. (b) Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I. (c) That Kanchi had Buddhist monasteries, Hindu temples and many Jains, and that its people valued honesty and learning, since these do not depend on exact counts. (d) A reasoned decision, e.g. print the faiths and the quotation but flag the numbers as likely exaggerated, or leave the numbers out.
s: Part (a): Xuanzang and Kanchipuram
Part (b): Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I
Part (c): the mix of faiths and the character of the people
Part (d): decision about the numbers with a reason

questions.q: A student labels a timeline card, 'The Cholas were reborn in the 9th century under Aditya I, who founded Tanjavur.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the Cholas were reborn under Vijayalaya in the 9th century, with his new capital at Tanjavur. His son Aditya I expanded the kingdom by defeating the Pallavas. Madurai was the Pandya capital, and the rebirth is placed in the 9th century.
o: Vijayalaya founded Tanjavur; Aditya I was his son
Aditya I was Vijayalaya's father and the first Chola
Tanjavur should be Madurai, the Pandya capital
The rebirth should be in the 10th century

questions.q: Aditya I overthrew the Pallavas in the late 9th century and Chola dominance lasted until the 13th century, so the Cholas dominated south India for about ___ centuries after that conquest.
A guide in Madurai tells tourists, 'You are standing in the capital that Vijayalaya chose for the Cholas.' What is the right correction?
questions.a: Madurai was the capital of the Pandyas, a vibrant cultural centre, while Vijayalaya's new Chola capital was Tanjavur (Thanjavur). The Cheras held the Kerala coast and the Pallavas ruled from Kanchi.
o: Madurai was Pandya; Tanjavur was the Chola capital
Madurai was the Chera capital on the Kerala coast
Madurai was the Pallava capital before Kanchi
Nothing; Vijayalaya moved the Chola capital to Madurai

questions.q:
Match each kingdom in Column A with what the chapter tells us about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Pandyas  2. Cholas  3. Cheras  4. Pallavas
Column B: a. kept their independence along the Kerala coast  b. a copper plate mentions their translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil  c. overthrown by Aditya I in the late 9th century  d. known for an efficient administration and a powerful navy
questions.a: The Pandyas' Mahabharata translation is known from a copper plate (b); the Cholas were known for administration and navy (d); the Cheras kept their independence (a); the Pallavas were overthrown by Aditya I (c). The distractors swap the Cholas with the Pandyas or the Cheras with the Pallavas.

questions.q: A guide in the Thanjavur bronze gallery points to an early Chola Nataraja, 'Lord of dance', and says it shows what the dynasty valued. Which statement from the chapter does the sculpture best support?
questions.a: The Cholas patronised arts such as sculpture and architecture. The Pandyas ruled from Madurai, the Cheras kept the Kerala coast independent, and Aditya I is credited with defeating the Pallavas, not with sculpture.
o: The Cholas patronised sculpture and architecture
The Pandyas ruled the Kaveri delta from Thanjavur
The Cheras built the empire's largest navy
Aditya I made sculpture the Pallavas' chief art

questions.q: Karthik's family farms near Kumbakonam in the Kaveri delta. His teacher asks why the Chola heartland stayed so prosperous. Which reason is in the chapter?
questions.a: The fertile Kaveri delta together with efficient irrigation techniques gave a steady agricultural output. Gold mines, timber from Himalayan forests and annual tribute from the Pallavas are not given as the reason.
o: Delta soil and efficient irrigation gave steady crops
Rich gold mines in the Kaveri delta paid for the empire
A trade in timber from the Himalayan forests
Tribute from the Pallavas collected every year

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Madurai, the capital of the Cholas, was a vibrant cultural centre.
2. The Cheras, along the Kerala coast, were conquered and ruled by the Pandyas.
3. Aditya I, son of Vijayalaya, expanded Chola power by defeating the Pallavas.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 3 is correct. Madurai was the Pandya capital and the Cholas ruled from Tanjavur. The Cheras maintained their independence.
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Pandya, Chola and Chera kingdoms were already mentioned in an edict of Ashoka as his southern neighbours.
Reason (R): In the period of this chapter they re-emerged and shaped the political and cultural life of the South.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true: the chapter says the three kingdoms were named in an edict of Ashoka nearly a millennium earlier, and that they re-emerged in this period. The re-emergence happened centuries later and does not explain why Ashoka named them.

questions.q: True or False: The Cholas defeated the Pallavas in the late 9th century, swept aside the Pandyas in the 10th and remained dominant in south India until the 13th century. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Aditya I defeated the Pallavas, the mighty Cholas swept the Pandyas aside in the 10th century, and the chapter says Chola dominance in south India lasted until the 13th century.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Aditya I over the Pallavas, the Pandyas swept aside in the 10th century, dominance till the 13th century

questions.q: Lakshmi reads in a museum that a copper plate mentions a translation of the Mahabharata into Tamil. (a) Which kingdom, with which capital, is the copper plate speaking of? (b) Why can we not read that translation today?
questions.a: (a) The Pandyas, with their capital at Madurai. (b) The chapter says the translation has unfortunately not survived; we know of it only from the copper plate.
s: Part (a): the Pandyas, capital Madurai
Part (b): the translation has not survived

questions.q: (a) Whom did Aditya I defeat, and what did the Cholas gain from the victory? (b) In which century did this happen, and was it before or after the Pandyas were swept aside?
questions.a: (a) He defeated the Pallavas, bringing most of present-day Tamil Nadu and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh under Chola control. (b) In the late 9th century, which is before the 10th century when the Cholas swept the Pandyas aside.
s: Part (a): the Pallavas defeated; most of Tamil Nadu and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh gained
Part (b): late 9th century, so before the Pandyas were swept aside in the 10th

questions.q: True or False: Swept aside by the Cholas in the 10th century, the Pandyas never recovered. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Pandyas were swept aside by the mighty Cholas in the 10th century, but they would re-emerge some three centuries later.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they re-emerged some three centuries later

questions.q: Explain how two languages were used in a land grant inscription of this period, and suggest one reason for using two.
questions.a: The ruler and his dynasty were praised in Sanskrit, while the operative details of the grant were recorded in the local language. A reasoned suggestion, e.g. Sanskrit gave the grant prestige while the local language let the people concerned understand it.
s: Sanskrit for praise, local language for operative details
A reasonable explanation for using both

questions.q: Imran says, 'The Pandyas, Cholas and Cheras were often at war with each other, so the Cheras must have been absorbed by their stronger neighbours.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter does say the southern kingdoms were often at war with each other, but it states that the Cheras, also known as Chera Perumals, maintained their independence along the Kerala coast despite their neighbours' military power. The chapter says little more about them, but it gives no sign of absorption.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since the Cheras were not absorbed
Accepts the true part: the southern kingdoms were often at war
Cites the Cheras keeping independence on the Kerala coast despite neighbours' power

questions.q: Compare the Pandyas and the Cholas on three points: where they were strong, how they traded or built, and how their fortunes changed.
questions.a: The Pandyas controlled much of southern Tamil Nadu with Madurai as capital, while the Cholas held the Kaveri delta with Tanjavur as capital. The Pandyas traded with Southeast Asia through Korkai and built rock-cut temples; the Cholas had a powerful navy and grand temples. The Pandyas were swept aside by the Cholas in the 10th century but re-emerged three centuries later, while the Cholas were dominant until the 13th century.
s: Region and capital of each
Trade, navy or building of each
Change in fortunes over the centuries

questions.q: An answer key says: 'Because the fertile delta and efficient irrigation ensured a steady agricultural output.' Write the question to which this is the answer, and name two other things for which the dynasty was known.
questions.a: Question: Why did the Chola heartland remain prosperous? Other things: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy and grand temples (any two).
s: A suitable question matching the answer
First other feature of the Chola empire
Second, different feature

questions.q: Compare the Pandyas, the Cheras and the Cholas on capital or region, trade and culture, and fortunes in this period. Then analyse what contributed to the Cholas building the biggest empire.
questions.a: The Pandyas ruled southern Tamil Nadu from Madurai, traded with Southeast Asia through Korkai and patronised poets; the Cholas swept them aside in the 10th century. The Cheras held the Kerala coast and maintained their independence. The Cholas, reborn under Vijayalaya with Tanjavur as capital, expanded under Aditya I, who defeated the Pallavas. The Cholas' empire was helped by (the chapter lists these features and does not say one alone caused it): the fertile Kaveri delta and efficient irrigation, an efficient administration and a strong navy.
s: Pandyas: capital, trade, culture
Cheras: Kerala coast and independence
Cholas: Vijayalaya, Tanjavur, Aditya I
How fortunes differed
Analysis of Chola strengths: agriculture, administration, navy

questions.q: 'The Cholas ended up building one of the largest empires in south Indian history.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: The Cholas were reborn under Vijayalaya in the 9th century with a new capital at Tanjavur. His son Aditya I defeated the Pallavas and brought most of present-day Tamil Nadu and parts of southern Andhra Pradesh under Chola control. They were known for an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy and grand temples, and they patronised sculpture and architecture and promoted Tamil and Sanskrit. The fertile Kaveri delta with efficient irrigation ensured steady agricultural output. Their dominance lasted until the 13th century.
s: Rebirth under Vijayalaya and Tanjavur
Aditya I's conquests
Administration, navy, temples
Arts and languages, and agriculture
Duration of dominance until the 13th century

questions.q:
A museum in Madurai is planning a timeline wall. A volunteer places two cards: 'Pandyas rise to power (6th century)' and 'The Pandyas are swept aside (10th century)'. The director asks her to finish the story.
(a) Which dynasty swept the Pandyas aside, and from which capital did that dynasty rule?
(b) In which century do the Pandyas re-emerge?
(c) Name two features for which the dynasty of part (a) became known.
(d) The wall has room for a large panel on only one of the two dynasties. Which should it be? Decide and justify with the dates from the timeline and your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Cholas, from Tanjavur. (b) The 13th century, about three centuries after the 10th. (c) Any two: an elaborate and efficient administration, a powerful navy, grand temples. (d) Either choice is acceptable if justified: the Pandyas rose by the 6th century, were swept aside in the 10th and re-emerged in the 13th, a story of return; the Cholas were dominant until the 13th century with their administration, navy and temples.
s: Part (a): Cholas and Tanjavur
Part (b): 13th century
Part (c): two features such as administration, navy, temples
Part (d): panel chosen and justified with dates and features

questions.q:
A Chola-era copper plate records a grant of a village to a temple. Its opening lines praise the king and his family in one language, while the later lines, which list the fields and what each family must pay, are in another language. A farmer of the village can read only the second language.
(a) Name the two languages.
(b) Name the Chola capital and the king who founded it as his new capital in the 9th century.
(c) What does the use of both languages show about the Cholas' attitude to literature?
(d) A village panchayat in Tamil Nadu must choose between writing every notice twice, in a formal language and in the local language, which costs more, or writing it once in the formal language only. Using the Chola practice, decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit and Tamil. (b) Tanjavur, made the capital by Vijayalaya. (c) They promoted Tamil as well as Sanskrit literature. (d) A reasoned decision: writing twice costs more but, as in the Chola grants, the operative details reach those affected in the local language while the formal language gives the ceremonial praise; writing once saves money but farmers who cannot read the formal language lose the details.
s: Part (a): Sanskrit and Tamil
Part (b): Tanjavur and Vijayalaya
Part (c): Cholas promoted Tamil as well as Sanskrit
Part (d): decision weighing cost against readers, with the Chola practice

questions.q: In a 9th-century village, a chief receives a large land grant but never ploughs a field himself. Which situation does the chapter say this fits?
questions.a: The chapter says the land grant system expanded greatly and created a new class of landholders, many of whom did not till the land themselves, so powerful intermediaries often exploited peasants. It does not say grants were limited to cultivators or royal kin, or that they ended.
o: Many holders did not till the land themselves
Grants were made only to those who tilled the soil
Land grants came to an end in this period
All grants went to members of the royal family

questions.q: A kingdom is divided into 4 provinces, each province into 5 districts and each district into 10 villages. The kingdom has ___ villages in all.
Aarti writes, 'In the 9th century every village was run by officers posted from the capital.' Which fact from the chapter lets her teacher correct this?
questions.a: The chapter says villages, the lowest administrative units, were overseen by headmen, accountants and local committees and remained largely self-governed. Samantas were subordinate rulers over regions, and dvarapanditas were gatekeepers in universities.
o: Villages largely governed themselves under local committees
Villages were governed by samantas posted from the capital
Villages were run by scholar gatekeepers of the monasteries
Villages had no officials because kings ruled them directly

questions.q: A vassal chief led the army and managed local administration for his overlord. When the overlord's central authority weakened, the vassal became powerful enough to overthrow him. Which dynasty in the chapter followed this path?
questions.a: The Rashtrakutas, once samantas under the Chalukyas. The Palas were chosen by the people, the Pallavas were overthrown by the Cholas, and the Pratiharas were finally eliminated by the Ghaznavids.
o: The Rashtrakutas
The Palas
The Pallavas
The Gurjara-Pratiharas

questions.q: A 9th-century inscription in a Tamil village records that a landholder paid for a new tank. What does the chapter say such sponsorship did for the donor?
questions.a: It raised his social status, in addition to helping irrigation. The chapter does not link it with command of the army, tax freedom or becoming a samanta.
o: It raised his social status
It put him in command of the army
It freed him from paying any tax
It made him a samanta of the king

questions.q:
Read the statements about administration and land in this period.
1. Provinces were called mandalas and districts were called bhuktis.
2. The land grant system that began under the Guptas expanded greatly.
3. Many inscriptions record the sponsorship of a well, pond or tank, which raised the donor's social status.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: provinces were bhuktis or rashtras and districts were mandalas.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls the varna-jati system of this period flexible rather than rigid.
Reason (R): Several sources indicate that the Palas and the Kakatiyas were originally Shudras but in time came to be regarded as Kshatriyas.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: dynasties moving from Shudra to Kshatriya status is one of the chapter's examples of how the system varied and was flexible.

questions.q:
Match each term or name in Column A with Column B.
Column A: 1. Samanta  2. Mandala  3. Kayastha  4. Tribhuvana Mahadevi I
Column B: a. a district  b. a vassal or tributary ruler  c. scribes who became a distinct jati in the 10th century  d. a 9th-century queen of the Bhauma-Karas of present-day Odisha
questions.a: A samanta is a vassal (b); a mandala is a district (a); the Kayasthas, scribes and clerks, became a jati in the 10th century (c); Tribhuvana Mahadevi I was the Bhauma-Kara queen (d). Distractors swap the first two terms, which are both administrative.

questions.q: True or False: Once the large empires fell, Indian society of this period became mostly urban, because trade and markets flourished. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that, although trade and markets flourished, Indian society remained largely rural and agrarian during this period.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: society remained largely rural and agrarian despite flourishing trade

questions.q: (a) In what two ways were samantas indispensable to a king? (b) Why could a king still not depend on them fully?
questions.a: (a) They led armies and managed local administration. (b) Their loyalty could be fragile, especially when they felt the central authority was weakening, as the Rashtrakutas, once samantas of the Chalukyas, showed by overthrowing their overlords.
s: Part (a): led armies and managed local administration
Part (b): loyalty fragile when the centre weakened, with the Rashtrakuta example

questions.q: Tribhuvana Mahadevi I of the Bhauma-Karas issued land grants under the title 'Paramabhattarika Maharajadhiraja'. (a) In which century did she rule, and what does the title mean? (b) Why is such a grant useful evidence about women in this period?
questions.a: (a) She ruled in the 9th century; the title means 'supreme sovereign empress, great queen of the three worlds'. (b) It shows that a woman held full royal authority and issued grants in her own name, one of several queens who ascended the throne in this period.
s: Part (a): 9th century; supreme sovereign empress, great queen of the three worlds
Part (b): a woman ruling in her own name, so women could hold royal power

questions.q: A merchant of the 9th century wants to sell goods in Chinese ports and also in ports in present-day Iran and Iraq. (a) Which coast of India should he sail from for each destination? (b) Which other regions does the chapter name on the route he takes to China?
questions.a: (a) For Chinese ports he should use the east coast; for Iran and Iraq the west coast. (b) The east coast connected with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, all the way to Chinese ports.
s: Part (a): east coast for China, west coast for Iran and Iraq
Part (b): Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia on the east-coast route

questions.q: Meghna says, 'In this period women appear only as queens.' Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter that show she is wrong.
questions.a: In Bana's Harshacharita women take part in agriculture and crafts and serve in courts as entertainers, musicians, storytellers and attendants; many inscriptions record women making offerings to temples or having water structures built.
s: First valid evidence of women outside queenship
Second valid and different evidence

questions.q: A column in a school magazine claims: 'When the big empires fell, the cities of India declined everywhere.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says some historians suggested urban decline but the evidence is more complex. In north India most older cities stayed occupied and new ones emerged; Xuanzang noted the decline of Kaushambi and Shravasti but described thriving Sthaneshvara, Kanyakubja and Kashi. In south India cities flourished, with temples as centres of commerce and ports fuelling maritime trade. 'Everywhere' is wrong.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'everywhere'
North India: older cities occupied, new ones emerged, with Xuanzang's examples
South India: temples and ports sustained cities

questions.q: Use the example of the Kayasthas to explain how an occupational group could turn into a jati.
questions.a: The Kayasthas were historically scribes or clerks, a professional group open to different varnas. In the 10th century they became a distinct jati. In parts of Bengal, Brahmana surnames such as Vasu, Ghosha, Datta and Dama came to be associated with them, showing a fusion of Brahmana and non-Brahmana families, and over time they married mainly within their group.
s: Began as a professional group of scribes open to different varnas
Fusion of Brahmana and non-Brahmana families, e.g. surnames
Marriage within the group made them a jati in the 10th century

questions.q: A textbook note says, 'The varna-jati system of this period was fixed and rigid.' Using three facts from the chapter, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says varna and jati were flexible. The Palas and the Kakatiyas, originally Shudras, came to be regarded as Kshatriyas. New jatis multiplied, based on occupation or region, and tribes and foreign migrants were absorbed into the system. Several bhakti saints were Shudras, and different varnas cooperated economically.
s: States that the chapter calls the system flexible
Palas and Kakatiyas rising from Shudra to Kshatriya status
Another valid fact, e.g. absorption of tribes or the multiplication of jatis

questions.q: 'The expansion of land grants brought both benefits and costs.' Justify this statement.
questions.a: The land grant system that began under the Guptas expanded greatly, with land given to individuals, communities and religious establishments, creating a new class of landholders. Many grants aimed to bring uncultivated land under cultivation, which expanded agriculture and crop diversity. Irrigation works such as the tanks built by the Pallavas supported better farming, and irrigation and agricultural growth supported agro-based crafts and industries. The costs were that many holders did not till the land and powerful intermediaries often exploited peasants. Sponsoring wells, ponds and tanks also raised the donor's status.
s: Origin under the Guptas and the new class of landholders
Benefit: more cultivated land and crop diversity
Benefit: irrigation and agricultural growth supporting crafts and industries
Cost: holders who did not till, exploitation of peasants
A balanced conclusion or the status gained by donors

questions.q: Explain how a king of this period ruled his core regions and distant regions, and analyse one advantage and one challenge of this system.
questions.a: Kings like the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas ruled their core regions directly, dividing them into provinces, districts and villages with officials at every level, and governed other regions through samantas. Villages were largely self-governed under headmen, accountants and local committees, and south India saw assemblies at several levels. The advantage was that samantas led armies and ran local administration, so the king need not control every region. The challenge was that their loyalty could be fragile when the centre looked weak, as when the Rashtrakutas overthrew the Chalukyas.
s: Direct rule of the core regions
Rule through samantas elsewhere
Levels of administration and the self-governing village
An advantage of the system
A challenge with the Rashtrakuta example

questions.q:
A guild of ship-owning merchants runs 30 ships: 12 on its west-coast route and 18 on its east-coast route. A merchant shows the board to a Class 7 group and says the guild can afford one new ship this year.
(a) From which century did the west coast see brisk shipping with ports in West Asia and Africa?
(b) Besides ports, what does the chapter say acted as centres of commerce in the cities of south India?
(c) What do the Chera copper-plate inscriptions mention, and what does it show about India?
(d) Should the new ship go to the west or the east route? Decide, using the guild's 12 and 18 ships and what the chapter says about both coasts.
questions.a: (a) The 8th century. (b) Temples. (c) The presence of Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders from West Asia, showing India as a hub of international trade. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the east already has 18 of the 30 ships and reaches Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China, while the west has only 12 but a brisk trade with Iran, Iraq and East Africa, so adding there balances the guild.
s: Part (a): 8th century
Part (b): temples as centres of commerce
Part (c): Christian, Muslim and Jewish traders, India as an international hub
Part (d): decision justified with the ship numbers and the chapter

questions.q:
On a temple wall in a Tamil Nadu village, a long 10th-century inscription lays down how the members of the village council are to be chosen. A Class 7 group compares it with the way their own school council is selected. The teacher adds that the village's daily affairs were handled by people with local knowledge.
(a) Name the dynasty that issued the inscription and the council it describes.
(b) What does the chapter say such evidence shows about democratic traditions in India?
(c) Name two officials or bodies who oversaw a village.
(d) The Uttaramerur rules were cut in stone where all could read them, and they are still known after a thousand years. Would a school council be better served by written rules on the notice board or by unwritten custom? Give one advantage and one difficulty of writing rules down, and decide.
questions.a: (a) The Cholas; the village sabha at Uttaramerur. (b) A long continuity of democratic traditions, going back some 1,500 years to the janapadas. (c) Any two of headmen, accountants and local committees. (d) A reasoned decision: public written rules, like the inscription, make selection clear and lasting, but they may be rigid or hard for some to read; custom is flexible but easily forgotten or disputed. Either choice is acceptable if justified.
s: Part (a): Cholas and the village sabha
Part (b): continuity of democratic traditions back to the janapadas
Part (c): two valid officials or bodies
Part (d): advantage, difficulty and a decision

questions.q: Brahmagupta was born in 598 CE and Harsha's rule at Kannauj began in 606 CE, so Brahmagupta was born ___ years before Harsha's rule began.
A Class 7 student learns the rules for adding and multiplying with zero, negative numbers and fractions. According to the chapter, whose work introduced these rules?
questions.a: The chapter says Brahmagupta, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, introduced the rules of arithmetic operations with zero, negative numbers and fractions, 'the same that you now learn at school'. Bhaskara I worked on trigonometry, Mahavira wrote the first mathematics work independent of astronomy, and Virahanka established the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence.
o: Brahmagupta
Bhaskara I
Mahavira
Virahanka

questions.q: A quiz asks for the Jain scholar at Amoghavarsha's court who wrote the first mathematics work independent of astronomy. A student answers, 'Mahavira, the great Jain teacher.' What is the right correction?
questions.a: The chapter says the mathematician Mahavira lived at the court of Amoghavarsha Nripatunga and is not to be confused with the great Jain teacher Mahavira, who lived over a millennium earlier. Brahmagupta and Virahanka were other scholars of the period.
o: A different man: the mathematician came later
The same man: the teacher also wrote mathematics
Brahmagupta, who lived at the same royal court
Virahanka, the finder of the Fibonacci sequence

questions.q: Over some centuries a village goddess of a hill district becomes identified with a wider devi, and her local myths are retold in a Purana. Which process from the chapter does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says the Puranas, with their elaborate mythology and sacred geography, helped integrate local deities and regional myths into broader pan-Indian cults, especially those of Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna and various devis. The other options describe different developments in the chapter.
o: Puranas fitting local deities into pan-Indian cults
The Alvars carrying hymns from the South to the North
Tantric schools replacing temple worship
Monks of Vikramashila spreading Tibetan Buddhism

questions.q: On a school tour of Karnataka, Diya sees a tall 10th-century monolithic statue of a figure in deep meditation, with an anthill behind him and plants climbing his arms. Which tradition does it belong to?
questions.a: Jainism: this is the monolithic Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, a revered Jain figure shown in a meditation lasting 12 years. Bhakti, Tantric and Vedic traditions are not linked with it.
o: Jainism
The Alvar bhakti tradition
The Tantric tradition
The Vedic sacrifice tradition

questions.q: In a Tamil temple town, a woman devotee called Andal composes hymns in Tamil to Vishnu. To which group of poet-devotees does she belong?
questions.a: The Alvars, the devotees of Vishnu; Andal was one of them. The Nayanars worshipped Shiva, and the other two options are not groups of devotional poets.
o: The Alvars
The Nayanars
The dvarapanditas
The Kashmir Shaivas

questions.q:
Read the statements about religion in this period.
1. The 12 Alvars were devotees of Shiva and the 63 Nayanars were devotees of Vishnu.
2. The initial spark of the bhakti spread came from the South, in devotional literature written in Tamil.
3. Tantric schools emerged around the 6th century and rejected all rituals in favour of silent devotion.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. Statement 1 swaps the deities: the Alvars were devotees of Vishnu and the Nayanars of Shiva. Statement 3 is false: the Tantric schools emphasised rituals, meditation, mantras and the worship of powerful deities, especially Shakti.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhakti poetry reached people across gender and social divisions and reshaped Indian society and literature.
Reason (R): Bhakti poetry, composed mostly in regional languages, invoked a direct personal relationship with the divine that was open to everyone.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because the poetry was in regional languages and offered a personal relationship with the divine open to everyone, it cut across gender and social divisions.

questions.q: True or False: Bhakti, as devotion addressed to a deity, existed long before the 6th century; what happened from the 6th century was its massive spread among all layers of society. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says bhakti did exist much earlier, but from the 6th century, rather than an organised movement, there was a massive spread across India and all layers of society, with the initial spark from the South.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: bhakti existed earlier; the new thing was its massive spread, sparked in the South

questions.q: (a) How many Alvars and Nayanars were there altogether? (b) Three of the Nayanars were women. What does the presence of women among the bhakti poets tell us about bhakti?
questions.a: (a) 12 + 63 = 75 devotees. (b) Bhakti was open to everyone and cut across gender and social divisions.
s: Part (a): 12 plus 63 gives 75
Part (b): bhakti cut across gender and social divisions

questions.q: In an 8th-century south Indian town, Shaivite devotees and Jain monks argue in public. A visitor concludes that the religious traditions of the period were enemies. (a) What fact in the chapter explains the argument? (b) Which statement in the chapter corrects the visitor's conclusion?
questions.a: (a) The chapter mentions occasional rivalries, such as between Shaivites and Jainas in south India. (b) The traditions coexisted peacefully most of the time, shared concepts such as dharma and karma, sacred spaces, motifs and sometimes deities, and rulers patronised all of them.
s: Part (a): occasional rivalry between Shaivites and Jainas
Part (b): peaceful coexistence most of the time, with shared concepts and patronage of all

questions.q: A student says, 'Mathematics in this period was only a tool for astronomy.' (a) Which scholar's work, according to the chapter, shows this is not wholly true? (b) What did most other mathematicians of the period concentrate on?
questions.a: (a) Mahavira, a Jain scholar at Amoghavarsha's court, authored the first work of mathematics independent of astronomy. (b) Refining astronomical calculation techniques, particularly to predict the positions of the planets at any given time.
s: Part (a): Mahavira and the first independent mathematics work
Part (b): refining astronomical calculations, such as predicting planetary positions

questions.q: At a festival in a Tamil temple town, a performer sings a Tamil hymn to Shiva composed by one of the three women among the saints of that tradition. (a) To which group of Tamil poet-devotees did she belong, and how many devotees did that group have? (b) Name the other group and the deity it worshipped.
questions.a: (a) The Nayanars (Nayanmars), 63 in number. (b) The Alvars, 12 devotees of Vishnu.
s: Part (a): Nayanars, 63 devotees
Part (b): Alvars, devotees of Vishnu

questions.q: Dev says, 'Buddhism declined all over India in this period because kings stopped supporting monasteries.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. In eastern India Buddhism thrived, partly influenced by Tantricism, especially under the Palas, whose monastic universities drew scholars from across Asia. Elsewhere it did decline, but because temple-based Hinduism and bhakti practices rose, not because rulers withdrew support; the chapter says rulers generally patronised several traditions.
s: Verdict: disagrees with 'all over India'
East: it thrived under the Palas and their monastic universities
Elsewhere: decline due to the rise of temple-based Hinduism and bhakti, not withdrawal of royal support

questions.q: Explain three ways in which Brahmagupta's work mattered, using the chapter.
questions.a: He introduced the rules of arithmetic operations with zero, negative numbers and fractions, the same ones students learn at school. He pioneered new techniques for solving certain equations, making him one of the founders of modern algebra. His works were translated into Persian and later Latin, contributing to the growth of mathematics in the Arab world and, later, Europe.
s: Rules for zero, negative numbers and fractions, still learnt at school
New techniques for solving equations, a founder of modern algebra
Translations into Persian and Latin carried his work to the Arab world and Europe

questions.q: Write a three-line diary entry of a villager in a Tamil temple town who hears a bhakti poet sing. Each line must use a different fact from the chapter about bhakti.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct facts, e.g. the poet sings in Tamil, a regional language; the hymn praises Vishnu or Shiva as a personal God; the poet may be a woman or come from any social background; devotion is open to everyone, not only to priests performing Vedic sacrifices.
s: Line 1 is correct and from the chapter
Line 2 is correct and different
Line 3 is correct and different again

questions.q: Describe how bhakti spread from the 6th century, covering its roots in the Puranas and temples, the southern spark, and its features. Then analyse its impact on society.
questions.a: The Puranas, with their mythology and sacred geography, integrated local deities into pan-Indian cults and stressed bhakti over Vedic sacrifices, centred on temples, mathas and pilgrimage sites. From the 6th century bhakti, which existed earlier, spread massively among all layers of society. The initial spark came from the South, where 12 Alvars (devotees of Vishnu, including the woman Andal) and 63 Nayanars (devotees of Shiva, including three women) produced Tamil devotional literature. Later saints from diverse backgrounds composed poetry in regional languages showing a direct personal relationship with the divine open to everyone. This cut across gender and social divisions, reshaped Indian society and literature, and its impact lingers today.
s: Roots in the Puranas, temples and pilgrimage
Spread from the 6th century across all layers of society
Alvars and Nayanars of the South
Features: regional languages, personal devotion open to all
Impact: cut across gender and social divisions, reshaped literature

questions.q: 'India built an unrivalled knowledge tradition in mathematics and astronomy.' Justify this using the scholars of this period and the purposes of their work.
questions.a: Brahmagupta introduced rules for arithmetic with zero, negative numbers and fractions and new techniques for solving certain equations, and his works reached the Arab world and Europe through Persian and Latin. Bhaskara I did pioneering work in trigonometry and wrote a commentary on the Aryabhatiya. Virahanka was the first to establish the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence. Mahavira wrote the first work of mathematics independent of astronomy. Others refined astronomical calculations to predict planetary positions. The tradition ran from Aryabhata and Varahamihira to Bhaskaracharya, was driven by both pure inquiry and practical aims like calendars and eclipse predictions, and needed royal patronage.
s: Brahmagupta and the spread of his work
Bhaskara I and Virahanka
Mahavira and astronomical refinements
The long tradition before and after
Purposes (calendars, eclipses) and royal patronage

questions.q:
A school tour of Karnataka and Maharashtra stops at a tall monolithic statue made in the 10th century. The guide says it shows a revered figure meditating for 12 years until an anthill rose behind him and plants climbed his limbs. The leader has time to add one more stop and must choose between a Pallava rock-cut site in Tamil Nadu and Ellora in Maharashtra, to support the theme 'rulers supported many faiths'.
(a) Name the statue and the town where it stands.
(b) Name the Pallava place where the chapter says rock-cut caves and monolithic temples were carved.
(c) Name two places in the chapter that have Jain cave temples.
(d) Which extra stop, the Pallava site or Ellora, better supports the theme? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Bahubali, at Shravanabelagola. (b) Mamallapuram. (c) Ellora and Badami. (d) Ellora is a strong choice because it holds both the Hindu Kailashanatha temple and Jain cave temples, patronised by the Rashtrakutas who supported Hindu, Buddhist and Jain schools; the Pallava site shows patronage of Jain, Vaishnavite and Shaivite schools through its rock-cut caves. A reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): Bahubali and Shravanabelagola
Part (b): Mamallapuram
Part (c): Ellora and Badami
Part (d): choice justified with a chapter fact

questions.q:
A maths club prepares a poster: 'Born in 598 CE in the city that was the first capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, he set down rules for arithmetic with zero, negative numbers and fractions. His books were later read in the Arab world and then in Europe.' The club wants to name its Maths Day after one of the scholars of this period.
(a) Name the scholar and the city.
(b) Name one other contribution of this scholar to mathematics, besides the rules on the poster.
(c) Through which two languages did his works reach the Arab world and Europe?
(d) Should the day be named after this scholar or after Mahavira, who wrote the first work of mathematics independent of astronomy? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Brahmagupta; Bhillamala (modern Bhinmal). (b) He pioneered new techniques for solving certain equations, making him one of the founders of modern algebra. (c) Persian and later Latin. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: Brahmagupta's rules for zero and negatives are the ones school students use and his work travelled widely; Mahavira marks mathematics becoming a subject independent of astronomy.
s: Part (a): Brahmagupta and Bhillamala
Part (b): techniques for solving equations, founder of modern algebra
Part (c): Persian and Latin
Part (d): decision justified from the chapter

questions.q: At Mandsaur a guide says, 'These twin victory pillars were raised by a Gupta emperor after he beat Muhammad bin Qasim.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the twin vijayastambhas at Mandsaur commemorate the victory of the Aulikara king Yashodharma over a Huna leader; the Aulikara kings of Dashapura defeated the Huna leaders and effectively ended Huna power in India. The Arabs came to Sindh much later, in the 8th century.
o: They mark Aulikara king Yashodharma's win over a Huna leader
They mark Pratihara king Nagabhata I's win over a Huna leader
They mark Rashtrakuta king Krishna I's win over Huna raiders
They mark Gupta king Skandagupta's win over the Arab army

questions.q: Arab ships raided Thana, Bharuch and Debal in 637, but Sindh was conquered only in 712, which is ___ years after the raids.
A student says, 'Muhammad bin Qasim took Aror first, because it was King Dahar's capital, and only then Debal.' What is the right correction?
questions.a: The chapter says Debal fell first; from there bin Qasim moved eastward towards Aror (present-day Rohri in Sindh), the capital of King Dahar, who was killed in a fierce battle. Thana and Bharuch were only raided from the sea in 637.
o: Debal fell first; Aror came afterwards
Aror fell first, but Dahar escaped to Debal
Debal was Dahar's capital and Aror a port
He took Thana and Bharuch before either city

questions.q: Hamid wonders why the English word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mawsim' meaning 'season'. Which fact from the chapter helps him?
questions.a: India and Arabia were connected by trade long before the rise of Islam, with ships sailing with the monsoon winds and carrying goods, ideas and languages. The other options are not in the chapter.
o: Ships sailed with the monsoon winds long before Islam
Arabs ruled the whole west coast of India for three centuries
Sanskrit scholars settled in Baghdad in large numbers
The Hunas brought the word with them from Central Asia

questions.q: A Gwalior inscription says Nagabhata I 'crushed the large army of the powerful Mlechchha king'. A student says Mlechchha is the name of a dynasty. What does the chapter say the term came to mean?
questions.a: The chapter explains that Mlechchha originally referred to those who did not speak clearly or did not follow Vedic culture, and came to refer to foreigners. In this context it points to the Arab army that Nagabhata I met.
o: It came to refer to foreigners
It is the name of King Dahar's dynasty
It is a title of the Pratihara kings
It is a Huna word for a general

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. King Dahar of Aror was killed in battle by an arrow, after which his army was routed.
2. Within two years of Qasim's death, Indian chiefs rebelled and regained most of the conquered territory.
3. In Sindh, the Arab conquest replaced local institutions and led to mass conversions, as in their conquests elsewhere.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact compared with conquests elsewhere, and Hindus and Buddhists could rebuild temples and worship.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After about three centuries of effort, Arab dominion in India was limited to just two petty states, in Sindh and Punjab.
Reason (R): Indian rulers never joined hands against the Arabs.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: the geographer al-Istakhri observed this. R is false: the chapter says Indian rulers offered stubborn resistance and sometimes forged alliances to defeat the Arabs.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Aulikara king Yashodharma  2. Muhammad bin Qasim  3. Nagabhata I  4. Lalitaditya Muktapida
Column B: a. defeated an Arab chief three times, as the Rajatarangini says  b. crushed the large army of a 'Mlechchha king', as a Gwalior inscription says  c. led an Arab army into Sindh  d. commemorated by victory pillars at Mandsaur over a Huna leader
questions.a: Yashodharma's pillars at Mandsaur record victory over a Huna leader (d); Qasim led the army into Sindh (c); Nagabhata I crushed an Arab army (b); Lalitaditya defeated an Arab chief three times (a). Distractors swap the two Indian rulers who resisted the Arabs.

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the Hunas of Indian literature 'are thought to have been' a branch of the Huns. What does the wording tell you about the evidence? (b) Which dynasty's kings defeated two Huna leaders, and from which capital did they rule?
questions.a: (a) The link between the Hunas and the Huns of Central Asia is a reasoned belief, not a certainty. (b) The Aulikara dynasty, whose capital was Dashapura, modern Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh.
s: Part (a): 'thought to' shows the link is likely but not certain
Part (b): Aulikara dynasty, capital Dashapura (Mandsaur)

questions.q: (a) According to the Chachnama, how did Muhammad bin Qasim describe his reason for fighting King Dahar? (b) The Chachnama is a 13th-century Persian rendering of an older Arabic account. Why should a historian handle it with care as evidence for 712?
questions.a: (a) He said it was his bounden duty to carry on a religious war in obedience to the orders of God. (b) It was set down in Persian about five centuries after the events (13th century against 712 in the 8th) and is a rendering of an older account, so it is not an eyewitness record and should be checked against other sources.
s: Part (a): a bounden duty to carry on a religious war in obedience to God's orders
Part (b): written about five centuries later and a rendering of an earlier account, so needs cross-checking

questions.q: The Chachnama records that when King Dahar was killed, his widowed queen put up a brave resistance, and another queen ordered her treasure to be distributed among the brave soldiers. (a) What did the second queen's act aim to do? (b) What do the two accounts together suggest about how people responded to the invasion?
questions.a: (a) By giving her treasure to the brave soldiers she inspired them to stand against the invaders. (b) They suggest strong resistance by the local people, in which women also played a part in war.
s: Part (a): the gift of treasure inspired the soldiers to stand against the invaders
Part (b): local people resisted, and women had a role in warfare

questions.q: A temple priest in Sindh in the years after the conquest asks whether he may rebuild his temple and keep his share of the temple's revenue under the new rulers. (a) What does the chapter say the answer was? (b) How did this differ from what happened in some other regions that Islam reached?
questions.a: (a) Hindus and Buddhists were allowed to rebuild their temples and worship, and priests kept their share of revenue. (b) In other regions Islam replaced local institutions and led to mass conversions; the Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact.
s: Part (a): temples rebuilt and priests kept their revenue share
Part (b): elsewhere local institutions were replaced and mass conversions followed

questions.q: True or False: Arab scholars acknowledged the Indian origin of the decimal numerals with zero, even though the numerals became known in Europe as 'Arabic numerals'. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Arab mathematicians acknowledged the Indian origin of the system; it became known as 'Arabic' only because the Arabs transmitted it to Europe, and several dictionaries now add the term 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the Arabs acknowledged the Indian origin; the 'Arabic' name arose because they transmitted the numerals to Europe

questions.q: Sameer says, 'Every foreign invader who came to India in this period ended up as a part of Indian society.' Test his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says foreign invaders often assimilated and owned India's cultural traditions: the Hunas by the 7th century served as soldiers and in local administrations, used Sanskrit and Prakrit and adopted Gupta-style titles and coins. But 'every' is wrong: the chapter adds that with the advent of Islam the situation changed, and the Arabs struggled for a long time and kept only two petty states.
s: Verdict: partly right
The part that holds: the Hunas assimilated, with evidence
The part that fails: with Islam the situation changed, so not every invader assimilated

questions.q: Describe three forms of resistance the Arabs faced in India, with the person or dynasty for each.
questions.a: Indian chiefs rebelled within two years of Qasim's death and regained most of the territory. Nagabhata I of the Gurjara-Pratiharas crushed a large Arab army, according to a Gwalior inscription. Lalitaditya Muktapida of Kashmir defeated an Arab chief three times, according to the Rajatarangini. Rulers sometimes also forged alliances.
s: Revolt of Indian chiefs
Nagabhata I
Lalitaditya or alliances

questions.q: Write a three-line news bulletin dated 637 for a west-coast port, using three different facts from the chapter about the Arab naval raids, and make sure it does not claim that any territory was conquered.
questions.a: Any three correct, distinct facts, e.g. Muslim Arabs raided from the sea; the raids hit Thana, Bharuch and Debal; they did not secure lasting territorial control; the first attempts to conquer Afghan kingdoms were unsuccessful; Islam had spread far within a few years of Muhammad's death in 632.
s: Line 1 is correct and from the chapter
Line 2 is correct and a different fact
Line 3 is correct, new, and no conquest is claimed

questions.q: Compare the invasions of the Hunas and the Arabs in their origin, methods, resistance faced and long-term impact on India.
questions.a: The Hunas were nomads from Central Asia who attacked with horse-riding, archery and lightning-fast raids and pushed into the Ganga plains in the early 6th century; the Arabs came from the newly expanded Islamic world, first with naval raids in 637 and then with an army into Sindh under Muhammad bin Qasim. The Hunas were defeated by the Aulikara kings, while the Arabs were frustrated for centuries by the stubborn resistance of Indian rulers like Nagabhata I and Lalitaditya, and their dominion shrank to two petty states. The Hunas were assimilated into Indian society, adopting its language, titles and symbols. The Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact, though trade and the exchange of ideas such as the numerals continued.
s: Origin and methods of the Hunas
Origin and methods of the Arabs
Resistance each faced
Outcome for the Hunas: assimilation
Outcome for the Arabs: limited impact and cultural exchange

questions.q: 'The Arab conquest of Sindh had a limited political and religious impact.' Justify this statement from the chapter.
questions.a: Indian chiefs rebelled within two years of Qasim's death and regained most of the conquered territory. Further Arab advances into Rajputana and Malwa were short-lived because rulers like Nagabhata I crushed their armies and Lalitaditya defeated an Arab chief three times. Al-Istakhri observed that after three centuries their dominion was limited to two petty states in Sindh and Punjab, where they survived only by giving up iconoclasm and using native Hindus and Buddhists. In Sindh, Hindus and Buddhists were allowed to rebuild temples and worship, and priests kept their share of revenue. This contrasts with other regions where Islam replaced local institutions and led to mass conversions.
s: Revolt and recovery of territory
Short-lived gains and Indian victories
Al-Istakhri's observation about two petty states
Change in policy: temples and priests' revenue
Contrast with other regions

questions.q:
A 9th-century Arab merchant, Sulaiman, wrote about an Indian ruler: 'He maintains numerous forces, and no other Indian prince has so fine a cavalry. He is unfriendly to the Arabs; there is no greater foe of the Muslim faith than he. There is no country in India safer from robbers.' A Gwalior inscription of the same dynasty says one of its early kings crushed the large army of a 'Mlechchha king'.
(a) Name the dynasty and the early king.
(b) Why would an Arab merchant call the ruler a foe of his faith?
(c) What do the merchant's praise of the cavalry and of the roads suggest about how this dynasty ruled?
(d) A historian says the merchant's words can be trusted fully because he was a witness. Decide how far you agree, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Gurjara-Pratiharas; Nagabhata I. (b) The dynasty pushed back Arab invasions into northwest India, so the Arabs saw him as an enemy. (c) A strong, well-organised state with large forces that kept order, which also fits its success in resisting the Arabs. (d) Partly: he was an eyewitness and his facts match the Gwalior inscription, but he writes from the Arab side and as a merchant concerned with trade and safety, so his judgement should be checked against Indian sources. A reasoned view is accepted.
s: Part (a): Gurjara-Pratiharas and Nagabhata I
Part (b): the dynasty pushed back Arab invasions
Part (c): strong forces and order in the dynasty's rule
Part (d): reasoned judgement about an outsider's evidence

questions.q:
A museum places two coins side by side. One is a coin of the Huna ruler Toramana, with his name 'Tora' in Brahmi script; the other is a coin of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta. They look strikingly similar. A panel adds that a Huna is recorded on a temple's administration council in an inscription of the 7th century.
(a) The Hunas are thought to be a branch of which Central Asian people, and which dynasty defeated their leaders?
(b) Name the temple's administration council, and say what a Huna's presence on it tells us.
(c) Why do the two coins look so similar?
(d) The museum can afford one more exhibit: a model of a Huna cavalry raid of the early 6th century or a model of a temple council meeting of the 7th century. Choose one and justify with chapter evidence.
questions.a: (a) The Huns; the Aulikara kings of Dashapura. (b) The goshthika; it shows that the Hunas had assimilated into Indian society and held local roles. (c) The Hunas adopted Gupta-style royal titles, coin designs and religious symbols. (d) Either is acceptable if reasoned: the raid rests on their fast attacks that pushed deep into the Ganga plains in the early 6th century; the council meeting rests on their assimilation by the 7th century.
s: Part (a): the Huns, and the Aulikara kings who defeated them
Part (b): goshthika, showing assimilation and local roles
Part (c): Gupta-style coin designs adopted
Part (d): exhibit chosen and justified with chapter evidence
